summary: duplication/duplication-migration's semantic fingerprint matches on AST shape after identifier normalization, which can group functions that are structurally identical but reference distinct named values (different contracts, different constants) as one 'duplicate' family. Applying the migration then aliases every non-canonical function to the canonical one, discarding the distinct referenced value entirely.
detail: src/integrations/openai/{chat-completions,embeddings,models,responses}/codec.mts each define a one-line admission function of the shape `export function <name>(input: unknown): <WireType> { return <XContract>.assert(input, "<label>") as <WireType>; }`. 16 such functions share this shape and were reported as one semantic-duplication candidate (16 implementationVariants, 2916 removableBytes). The 16 functions each assert against a DIFFERENT named contract (openaiChatMessageContract, openaiChatToolCallContract, openaiChatFunctionToolContract, openaiResponseFormatContract, openaiUsageWireContract, openaiChatCompletionContract, openaiChatCompletionChunkContract, openaiEmbeddingsRequestContract, openaiEmbeddingContract, openaiEmbeddingsResponseContract, openaiModelWireContract, openaiModelsListResponseContract, openaiResponseRequestContract, openaiResponseFunctionToolContract, openaiResponseContract, plus openaiChatCompletionRequestContract itself as the chosen owner) — each contract validates a genuinely different OpenAI wire shape (a chat message vs. a tool call vs. a full request vs. a usage object, etc.). --apply rewrote all 15 non-owner declarations into `const <name> = openaiChatCompletionRequest; export { <name> };` (or an equivalent cross-file import alias), i.e. every caller of e.g. `openaiChatMessage(x)` now actually validates `x` against the full `/chat/completions` request schema instead of the single-message schema. This is a functional regression, not a deduplication: the 16 functions were never semantically the same operation, only syntactically the same shape with different free identifiers.
impact: Applying this candidate (or any future candidate of the same shape: a family of thin wrapper functions whose only difference is which named contract/constant they delegate to) silently breaks admission/validation for every caller of the non-owner names. The plan's own `applicable: true` / `refusals: []` gave no signal that the candidate was unsafe.
action_taken: Reverted immediately via `git checkout` before commit (all 7 touched files were uncommitted, so no broken state was ever committed or published). Not applied to any other candidate from this scan pending a fix to the fingerprinting/eligibility check below.
recommended_fix: duplication's semantic-fingerprint pass (or duplication-migration's own applicability check) should not treat two declarations as the same 'duplicate' family purely on AST shape after alpha-renaming of the declaration's own name; it must also compare (or refuse to alias across) the *other* free identifiers the body references — here, the contract/constant each function delegates its actual validation logic to. A thin wrapper `return CONTRACT.assert(input, label) as T` is only a true duplicate of another such wrapper when CONTRACT (and T) are the same referent, not merely the same shape of expression.
owner_note: Found while directly exercising duplication-migration per owner instruction ('stop cheating around what i said to do... Set up the tools') rather than continuing manual relocation. The instrument itself needs this fix before further --apply runs against real candidates can be trusted without a manual contract-identity check per candidate.
